articles.title: Sudan conflict: Peace efforts resume to end ‘drone war’ fuelling humanitarian crisis
articles.summary: Talks to halt the fighting in Sudan and alleviate the humanitarian crisis there continued in Geneva on Wednesday, where nearly two dozen countries convened to discuss a pathway to a ceasefire and transition to peaceful governance that represents all Sudanese people.
articles.content:
“Our first session, devoted to de-escalation, will offer an opportunity to explore practical ways forward,” said Pekka Haavisto, Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan, in a call to delegates to identify measures and use their “respective channels of engagement [to] build confidence and help create conditions conducive to a comprehensive ceasefire”.

Now in its fourth year, the conflict began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) – former allies who had jointly seized power in a 2021 coup.

Deadly drone attacks against civilians and public infrastructure have been a feature of the war and frequently condemned by humanitarian and human rights officials.

“The war in Sudan has become a drone war; it kills mostly civilians,” said Alexandre Fasel, State Secretary of Switzerland, which is co-hosting the meeting with the UN. “Famine-like conditions persist in Darfur, the Kordofan state and elsewhere in the country; it is the war that drives this hunger.”

Highlighting the protections offered to non-combatants by international law, Mr. Fasel insisted that the Geneva Conventions “are very clear: the protection of civilians and humanitarian access must not wait for a ceasefire and a political solution. Civilians are suffering and dying today.”

Millions in need

Across Sudan today, almost 34 million people need humanitarian support, according to the UN aid coordination office, OCHA, Mr. Fasel noted. He also cited UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) alerts that eight million Sudanese children are out of school today.

“This is not only a violation to the right of education but an immense risk factor for a future stable Sudan. Conflict-related sexual violence has re-emerged as a tactic to terrorise and humiliate the civilian population, often targeted along ethnicity or perceived affiliations,” he insisted.

In addition to discussing efforts towards a ceasefire, delegates are expected to consider a Sudanese-led “transitional political phase that reflects the aspirations” of the country’s people, by means of “an inclusive and credible dialogue”, the UN chief’s Personal Envoy, Mr. Havisto, said, insisting that “our role is to support the Sudanese in shaping their country’s shared future, with due regard for the diversity of their voices and experiences”.

Latest round of talks

The talks, known officially as Consultative Meetings on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives and Efforts in Sudan, have previously taken place in Cairo twice (June 2024 and January 2026) and in Djibouti (July 2024), Nouakchott (December 2024) and Brussels (June 2025) and Cairo (January 2026).

Neither the Sudanese Government nor the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are represented at the meeting in Geneva, as the mechanism was established for mediators to coordinate their actions.

On the margins of Wednesday’s meeting in Geneva, the UN Personal Envoy was also expected to engage with key regional and international partners from the so-called “Quad” mechanism” – involving the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt – and the “Quintet” mechanism of the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the UN, the European Union and the League of Arab States.

The current talks followed a day of humanitarian-focused discussions also at UN Geneva that involved delegations, senior UN officials and international non-governmental organizations operating in Sudan including the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the Sudan INGO Forum.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports on ongoing international peace efforts aimed at ending the deadly conflict in Sudan, which has caused severe humanitarian crises including civilian deaths, famine-like conditions, and disruption of education. The talks involve multiple countries and international organizations working towards a ceasefire and inclusive political transition, representing a significant and hopeful step towards peace and improved human rights for millions affected.
articles.personality_title: International talks resume to end Sudan’s deadly conflict and aid millions in need
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The conflict in Sudan began in April 2023 when two former allies, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), started fighting. This war has caused many deaths, especially from drone attacks, and created a severe humanitarian crisis with millions needing help.

**What happened** – On Wednesday, nearly 24 countries met in Geneva to discuss ways to stop the fighting and support a peaceful future for Sudan. These talks focus on finding a ceasefire and planning a political transition that includes all Sudanese people. The meeting is part of ongoing efforts that have taken place in several cities since 2024.

**Impact** – The conflict has caused famine-like hunger, damaged schools leaving 8 million children out of education, and increased violence against civilians. The talks in Geneva bring together important international groups to coordinate peace efforts and push for humanitarian access to those suffering. This cooperation shows a serious commitment to ending the crisis and helping millions of people.

**What's next step** – The peace talks will continue, with diplomats and organizations working to build trust and find practical solutions. The UN envoy will also meet with key countries involved in the region to strengthen support. The goal is to create a ceasefire and a fair political process led by Sudanese people.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Countries and organizations are working together in Geneva to stop the war in Sudan and support millions of civilians caught in the crisis.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les pourparlers internationaux reprennent pour mettre fin au conflit meurtrier au Soudan et aider des millions de personnes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le conflit au Soudan a commencé en avril 2023 lorsque deux anciens alliés, les Forces armées soudanaises (FAS) et les Forces de soutien rapide (FSR), ont commencé à s’affronter. Cette guerre a causé de nombreuses morts, surtout à cause des attaques de drones, et a créé une grave crise humanitaire avec des millions de personnes ayant besoin d’aide.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Mercredi, près de 24 pays se sont réunis à Genève pour discuter des moyens d’arrêter les combats et de soutenir un avenir pacifique pour le Soudan. Ces pourparlers visent à trouver un cessez-le-feu et à planifier une transition politique qui inclut tous les Soudanais. Cette réunion fait partie d’efforts continus qui ont eu lieu dans plusieurs villes depuis 2024.

**Impact** – Le conflit a provoqué une faim proche de la famine, endommagé les écoles laissant 8 millions d’enfants sans éducation, et augmenté la violence contre les civils. Les discussions à Genève rassemblent d’importants groupes internationaux pour coordonner les efforts de paix et pousser à l’accès humanitaire aux populations souffrantes. Cette coopération montre un engagement sérieux pour mettre fin à la crise et aider des millions de personnes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les pourparlers de paix vont continuer, avec des diplomates et des organisations travaillant à renforcer la confiance et à trouver des solutions pratiques. L’envoyé de l’ONU rencontrera aussi les pays clés de la région pour renforcer le soutien. L’objectif est de créer un cessez-le-feu et un processus politique juste dirigé par les Soudanais.

**En une phrase** – Des pays et des organisations travaillent ensemble à Genève pour arrêter la guerre au Soudan et soutenir des millions de civils pris dans la crise.
articles.personality_title_es: Reanudan conversaciones internacionales para acabar con el conflicto mortal en Sudán y ayudar a millones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El conflicto en Sudán comenzó en abril de 2023 cuando dos antiguos aliados, las Fuerzas Armadas de Sudán (SAF) y las Fuerzas de Apoyo Rápido (RSF), comenzaron a pelear. Esta guerra ha causado muchas muertes, especialmente por ataques con drones, y ha creado una grave crisis humanitaria con millones de personas que necesitan ayuda.

**Qué pasó** – El miércoles, casi 24 países se reunieron en Ginebra para discutir cómo detener los combates y apoyar un futuro pacífico para Sudán. Estas conversaciones buscan un alto al fuego y planear una transición política que incluya a todos los sudaneses. Esta reunión es parte de esfuerzos continuos que han ocurrido en varias ciudades desde 2024.

**Impacto** – El conflicto ha causado hambre parecida a la hambruna, dañado escuelas dejando a 8 millones de niños sin educación, y aumentado la violencia contra civiles. Las conversaciones en Ginebra reúnen a importantes grupos internacionales para coordinar esfuerzos de paz y facilitar ayuda humanitaria a los que sufren. Esta cooperación muestra un compromiso serio para acabar con la crisis y ayudar a millones.

**Próximo paso** – Las conversaciones de paz continuarán, con diplomáticos y organizaciones trabajando para construir confianza y encontrar soluciones prácticas. El enviado de la ONU también se reunirá con países clave de la región para fortalecer el apoyo. La meta es crear un alto al fuego y un proceso político justo liderado por los sudaneses.

**Una frase clave** – Países y organizaciones trabajan juntos en Ginebra para detener la guerra en Sudán y apoyar a millones de civiles atrapados en la crisis.

articles.title: Protest as a pillar of democracy
articles.summary: This spotlight is, then, a form of protest in its own right: a way of reasserting that protest is legitimate, important for democracy, and everywhere.
articles.content:
This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Democracy is often presented as an orderly, structured system of representation and deliberation, colorless and linear like an organizational version of the faux-classical architecture so many democratic countries adopt for their government buildings. Voting leads to representatives, debates lead to votes on laws, participation leads to action, like columns leading to a pediment.

But democracy is not actually about cushy debating chambers or political speeches — or not only about that. Democracy means rule by the people, and in most of the systems we call democracies today, the people’s role is for the most part narrowed to voting, and often a curtailed, difficult, limited vote that does little for accountability or expressing preferences on specific issues.

Protest is one of the ways we close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we have. With protest, the people can express general emotional responses or very specific policy proposals; we can punctuate the long intervals of electoral cycles to influence government outside of the voting booth; and perhaps most importantly, we build coalitions and solidarity, forming a collective consciousness of our democratic responsibilities.

Voting is a single, standardized, and fairly isolated action. Protest, on the other hand, unfolds in dozens, if not hundreds, of permutations, letting us — the people — express our creativity along with our civic engagement. One of the wonderful things about this spotlight has been seeing the sheer range of capacity and ingenuity as people use protest to inspire others, express anger or determination, and pressure governments and other decision-makers.

Maybe the most obvious example of this in the spotlight is the collaborative article on protest music, with its examples of not just different songs, but different styles and approaches and even understanding of what it means to use music for advocacy. In Japan, young people are finding new paths into activism, like handing out placards, while the Cockroach Janta Party in India has used memes and online jokes to mobilize young people right from the start of the movement.

Severe oppression requires more creativity, as this article about the evolution of street art in Russia points out. Similarly, Russians — many of them in exile — used allusion and wordplay in online videos to get their messages across.

That raises the question, ably explored in this piece, about whether online and offline protest are equally effective, and what their different strengths and weaknesses are. And, if the digital world has enabled new forms of protest, it has also activated new means of repression. Our friends at Ranking Digital Rights contributed this well-researched article about the complicity of telecoms in internet shutdowns in Africa. This piece, from AlgorithmWatch, details the Russian surveillance software being used against protesters in Georgia. And the virtual world can be used to hijack, undermine, or redirect protest energy, as this case study from Funky Citizens in Romania details.

As vibrant as protests are in the moment, though, it’s also important to ask about the long-term impact, the consequences, both good and bad. The protests in Bangladesh two years ago were successful in the sense that they led to a change of government; this article asks whether that change of government led to a meaningful difference in democratic accountability. And this powerful piece from Nepal follows up with those involved in the Gen Z protests there last year, tracking the long-term impacts of injuries and trauma.

As with all our monthly spotlights, this one is in many ways about showing the common threads that link all of our countries, as well as the exceptions that can open us to new ideas or inspire us to a different kind of action. This spotlight is, then, a form of protest in its own right: a way of reasserting that protest is legitimate, important for democracy, and everywhere.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the vital role of protest as a legitimate and creative form of democratic participation worldwide, emphasizing its broad societal significance in promoting accountability, civic engagement, and solidarity. It provides detailed examples from multiple countries and explores both the challenges and impacts of protest, offering substantial context and insight into its importance for democracy and human rights.
articles.personality_title: How protests keep democracy alive around the world
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Democracy is often seen as a simple system where people vote for leaders and laws are made in orderly ways. But in real life, democracy is more than just voting. It means people have a voice all the time, not just during elections.

**What happened** – A new series called “Protest in Democracy” by Global Voices explores how protests are a key part of democracy. It shows how people use many creative ways to protest, like music in Japan, memes in India, and street art in Russia. The series also looks at how governments try to stop protests, sometimes by cutting off internet access or using surveillance technology.

**Impact** – This series helps us understand that protests are an important way for people to express their ideas, feelings, and demands. Protests can bring people together and push governments to listen. The examples from different countries show how protests can be both powerful and creative, even when faced with challenges or danger.

**What's next step** – The series encourages more conversations about protests and their role in democracy. It also raises questions about how online and offline protests work differently and how new technology affects both protest and government control. This could lead to new ways to support peaceful protests and protect people’s rights.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Protests are a creative and essential way for people worldwide to take part in democracy beyond just voting.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment les manifestations maintiennent la démocratie dans le monde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La démocratie est souvent vue comme un système simple où les gens votent pour des dirigeants et où les lois sont faites de manière ordonnée. Mais en réalité, la démocratie, c’est plus que voter. Cela signifie que les gens ont une voix tout le temps, pas seulement pendant les élections.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Une nouvelle série appelée « Protestation en démocratie » par Global Voices explore comment les manifestations sont une partie clé de la démocratie. Elle montre comment les gens utilisent de nombreuses façons créatives de protester, comme la musique au Japon, les mèmes en Inde et l’art de rue en Russie. La série examine aussi comment les gouvernements tentent d’arrêter les manifestations, parfois en coupant l’accès à Internet ou en utilisant des technologies de surveillance.

**Impact** – Cette série nous aide à comprendre que les manifestations sont un moyen important pour les gens d’exprimer leurs idées, leurs sentiments et leurs demandes. Les manifestations peuvent rassembler les gens et pousser les gouvernements à écouter. Les exemples de différents pays montrent que les manifestations peuvent être à la fois puissantes et créatives, même face à des défis ou des dangers.

**Prochaine étape** – La série encourage plus de discussions sur les manifestations et leur rôle dans la démocratie. Elle pose aussi des questions sur la façon dont les manifestations en ligne et hors ligne fonctionnent différemment et comment la nouvelle technologie affecte à la fois les manifestations et le contrôle gouvernemental. Cela pourrait conduire à de nouvelles façons de soutenir les manifestations pacifiques et de protéger les droits des gens.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les manifestations sont un moyen créatif et essentiel pour les gens du monde entier de participer à la démocratie au-delà du simple vote.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo las protestas mantienen viva la democracia en todo el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La democracia suele verse como un sistema simple donde las personas votan por líderes y se hacen leyes de manera ordenada. Pero en la realidad, la democracia es más que solo votar. Significa que las personas tienen voz todo el tiempo, no solo durante las elecciones.

**Qué pasó** – Una nueva serie llamada «Protesta en la democracia» de Global Voices explora cómo las protestas son una parte clave de la democracia. Muestra cómo la gente usa muchas formas creativas de protestar, como la música en Japón, los memes en India y el arte callejero en Rusia. La serie también analiza cómo los gobiernos intentan detener las protestas, a veces cortando el acceso a internet o usando tecnología de vigilancia.

**Impacto** – Esta serie nos ayuda a entender que las protestas son una manera importante para que las personas expresen sus ideas, sentimientos y demandas. Las protestas pueden unir a la gente y presionar a los gobiernos para que escuchen. Los ejemplos de diferentes países muestran que las protestas pueden ser poderosas y creativas, incluso ante desafíos o peligros.

**Próximo paso** – La serie invita a más conversaciones sobre las protestas y su papel en la democracia. También plantea preguntas sobre cómo funcionan de manera diferente las protestas en línea y fuera de línea, y cómo la nueva tecnología afecta tanto a las protestas como al control gubernamental. Esto podría llevar a nuevas formas de apoyar las protestas pacíficas y proteger los derechos de las personas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las protestas son una forma creativa y esencial para que las personas de todo el mundo participen en la democracia más allá del voto.
